cim: Senate Assembly discusses student, faculty policies and artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: Senate Assembly discusses student, faculty policies and artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
The University of Michigan Senate Assembly met in the Alexander G. Ruthven Building Monday afternoon to discuss clinical faculty promotion criteria, the role of artificial intelligence in collegiate instruction and amendments to the University’s Board of Regents’ bylaws.

Information professor Kentaro Toyama, chair of the University’s Senate Advisory Committee on University Affairs, opened the meeting by introducing revisions to the promotion criteria for clinical faculty at the Medical School, with changes set to be implemented next academic year. Toyama said this was a top issue among SACUA discussions last semester and received largely positive feedback from faculty.

“The current system is apparently decades old, and involves criteria that were more relevant for the tenure track,” Toyama said. “There are family physicians who have remained ‘assistant clinical professors’ for decades. And so the new criteria has three different categories of clinical faculty, and also involves the ability for clinical faculty to be promoted based on a portfolio of accomplishments that are much more relevant to their actual clinical practice.”

While the adjustments have been positively received, clinical professor Terrill Bravender said this would only be a slight change to the system.

“I would caution against using the term ‘complete overhaul’ relating to the promotion criteria,” Bravender said. “I think the promotion criteria performed in the Medical School has been streamlined, and there’s a more expansive definition of what academic products are expected of our clinical faculty. But there’s still expectations for academic productivity.”

Next, Toyama provided updates regarding the Faculty Senate Student Relations Advisory Committee’s efforts to implement 28 amendments to the Statement of Student Rights and Responsibilities in 2025. Toyama said the amendments were proposed in response to the regents’ choice to unilaterally change disciplinary procedures relating to student protests in 2024.

“Many faculty interpreted (the regents’ changes) to have made it easier to punish pro-Palestine protesters,” Toyama said. “Whatever the politics, the legal analysis of these revisions suggests that in some cases they were unfair to students who were accused of violations and often violated basic principles of due process.”

The amendments were submitted to Martino Harmon, vice president for student life, and University President Domenico Grasso, who agreed to proceed with 22 of the amendments while he remains in office.

Next, in light of the University’s finalization of its guidelines for responsible and ethical AI use during the previous month’s meeting, the Senate Assembly heard from Tazin Daniels, associate director at the Center for Research of Leaning & Teaching.

Since 2023, the CRLT has supported faculty in examining the implications of generative AI for teaching and learning through facilitating seminars open to faculty across campus, as well as maintaining a blog for faculty advice. Daniels said the relationship between AI, students and faculty is complicated.

“We can all agree that academic integrity is vital to the work that all of us do and we want to make sure we hold the standards,” Daniels said. “At the same time, we understand the deeply troubling relationship that faculty are having now with transitioning from teaching and assessing students to policing and surveying students’ (AI usage).”

The Senate Assembly also talked about the role of AI in faculty work. History professor Derek Peterson, former SACUA chair, said faculty reliance on AI diminishes the need for specialized expertise.

“As a history professor, it strikes me as exceedingly injurious to actually evaluating students’ work,” Peterson said. “To me, it holds up the prospect of AI machines basically talking to each other, entirely eliminating human learning and human expertise. Why the hell do we have a university if we’re going to have machines evaluate each other’s AI capabilities?”

Francine Dolins, an associate psychology professor on the University’s Dearborn campus, said using AI to evaluate students’ work may require student consent.

“In terms of grading using AI, students are writing a piece, they’re submitting it and it’s their intellectual property,” Dolins said. “If we submit it, as faculty, into AI, then it’s opened up to the internet and anyone can access their intellectual property. Shouldn’t we ask the students? … I don’t want assignments being graded by AI for that very reason, because that’s intellectual property.”

Next, Faculty Senate Director Luke McCarthy presented proposed amendments to the regents’ bylaws.

The proposed amendments included “housekeeping” adjustments, such as eliminating language limiting Faculty Senate meetings in the winter semester and clarifying voting requirements for Faculty Senate members. McCarthy also proposed amendments considered as “substantive updates,” including eliminating SACUA’s nominating committee and granting emeritus faculty with at least 50% active employment voting privileges in the Faculty Senate.

By unanimous consent, the Senate Assembly further approved all amendments to move forward to the University Faculty Senate for a final vote at its upcoming Nov. 9 meeting. If approved, the amendments would move forward to be considered for consideration by the regents.

The meeting concluded with Toyama introducing a draft of a declaration of faculty rights and responsibilities initiated by SACUA.

“The idea is to have a relatively high-level document that indicates the rights that we believe all faculty should have, as well as responsibilities that we have as faculty,” Toyama said. “Think of it as our north star for any kind of issue that we are negotiating with the administration, from academic freedom and shared governance to compensation and benefits.”

The declaration is cycling through ongoing edits and projected to be completed and voted on by the Faculty Senate within this academic year.

Daily Staff Reporter Aliana Ritter can be reached at alianar@umich.edu.
